findings.headline: Key asset valuer retired October 2025; succession planning required for 2025/26 revaluation cycle
findings.detail: Moray Council's internal valuer, who also performs valuations for Grampian VJB, retired in October 2025. This is the second valuer retirement in recent years. Audit recommendation: Grampian VJB must ensure early discussion with the replacement valuer and auditors to ensure the new valuer understands audit responsibilities and can deliver timely valuations in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Loss of institutional knowledge and continuity risk in asset valuation; if replacement valuer is not properly briefed or available, the 2025/26 audit and asset valuation could be delayed
findings.figures: Two successive valuer retirements; Moray Council valuer also serves Grampian VJB
findings.quote: Moray Council's asset valuer, who also performs the valuation for Grampian VJB retired in October 2025 will be changing in 2025/26 and Grampian VJB will need to ensure there is replacement in place who can perform the revaluations exercise in 2024/25.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting performed incorrectly in arrears, errors below materiality threshold left unadjusted
findings.detail: First-year adoption of IFRS 16 in 2024/25 contained calculation errors: payments were computed in arrears rather than advance, resulting in right-of-use asset understated by £0.017 million and associated lease liability understated by £0.013 million. Management chose not to correct these errors because they fell below performance materiality of £0.093 million. The corrected calculations will be used in 2025/26 accounts.
findings.matters: Demonstrates process control gaps in implementing new accounting standards; unadjusted misstatements below materiality threshold can accumulate; indicates potential ongoing errors in lease valuation methodology
findings.figures: £0.017 million understatement of right-of-use asset; £0.013 million understatement of lease liability; performance materiality £0.093 million
findings.quote: We undertook audit work on the introduction of the right of use asset and liability and identified errors in the calculation due to payments being incorrectly calculated in arrears rather than in advance. This resulted in the right of use asset being understated by £0.017 million and the associated liabilities understated by £0.013 million. Grampian VJB have not amended for the errors identified as they were below performance materiality

findings.headline: Pension scheme accounting error corrected mid-audit, with asset ceiling capping pension asset at nil
findings.detail: The actuary (newly changed from Mercer to Hymans Robertson in 2024/25) identified a calculation error in benefits paid figures after draft accounts were submitted. This required revised IAS 19 and IFRIC 14 calculations. The IFRIC 14 assessment capped the pension asset at nil based on present value of economic benefits available. The error resulted in a decrease of £0.315 million to pension fund assets, though the asset ceiling calculation offset this impact on the statement of financial position.
findings.matters: Change in actuary and identification of material calculation errors suggests potential control weaknesses in pension valuation processes; the nil pension asset (rather than the £14.063 million asset after adjustment) is an unusual position indicating constrained benefit availability
findings.figures: £0.315 million decrease in pension assets due to actuary error; pension asset ceiling capped at £nil before adjustment to £14.063 million
findings.quote: Since the production of the draft financial statements, the Actuary notified Grampian VJB that an error had been made in the calculation of the benefits paid figures, therefore revised IAS19 calculations and a revised IFRIC14 assessment was provided to Grampian VJB. The figures were materially different

findings.headline: Absence of journal authorisation controls during 2024/25 audit period
findings.detail: The audit identified that Grampian VJB did not have journal authorisation processes in place during 2024/25, requiring additional audit procedures and testing to gain assurance over the control environment. While no material override was found, the absence of this fundamental control represents a governance weakness that was not addressed during the year.
findings.matters: Journal authorisation is a core control preventing unauthorised or erroneous entries to the general ledger; its absence increases risk of misstatement and indicates gaps in financial control design
findings.figures: No quantified impact, but audit required expanded procedures as alternative control testing
findings.quote: As Grampian VJB did not have journal authorisation processes in place during 2024/25, we were required to consider this in our journals assessment including mitigating and alternative controls, to gain assurance over the journal control environment.

findings.headline: Severe and persistent staffing vacancies creating operational risk and budgeting uncertainty
findings.detail: Grampian VJB has nine vacant posts as of October 2025, with four in the critical Valuation team. Staff vacancies have been described as 'an ongoing issue' causing significant underspends in employee costs (£0.412 million in 2024/25). Recruitment of qualified valuation staff is specifically identified as 'a key organisational risk'. The 2025/26 budget projects another £0.231 million underspend from the same cause, yet assumes 3% annual increases in employee costs based on expectation that vacancies will eventually be filled.
findings.matters: Persistent underfilled positions suggest inability to deliver planned services, uncertain cost structures making budget forecasts unreliable, and risk that the organisation cannot execute its core valuation function if staffing cannot be resolved
findings.figures: Nine vacant posts; £0.412 million underspend in employee costs 2024/25; £0.231 million projected underspend 2025/26; 3% annual assumed increases in employee costs despite historical vacancy pattern
findings.quote: A significant driver of the underspend is staff vacancies, which has been an ongoing issue for Grampian VJB for some time, due to difficulties in recruiting qualified valuation staff. Management recognise this challenge and recruitment of staff is a key organisational risk.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Plan for the Year Ending 2025-26 and Update on Recommendations from 2024-25
findings.headline: Internal Audit has issued a limited assurance opinion on governance and internal controls for four consecutive years.
findings.detail: The prior year audit recommendation notes that internal audit has delivered limited assurance opinions for four consecutive years, indicating fundamental weaknesses in governance, risk management and control frameworks. As of March 2026, concerns remain that audit recommendations from prior years are not being implemented. A significant IT system replacement (CareFirst) is underway with a planned go-live of 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: Persistent limited assurance opinions indicate systemic control weaknesses in the IJB; combined with financial stress and major system changes, this creates material risk of undetected errors, fraud or misappropriation.
findings.figures: Four consecutive years of limited assurance opinions (2022-23 through 2025-26)
findings.quote: This is the fourth year in succession that Internal Audit have provided a limited assurance opinion. Fundamentally, this indicates there are weaknesses in the framework of governance, risk management and control.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Plan for the Year Ending 2025-26 and Update on Recommendations from 2024-25
findings.headline: £3.133 million of identified 2025/26 savings plans have not been delivered.
findings.detail: The audit plan attributes the deteriorating financial position to non-delivery of approximately £3.133 million in planned savings, combined with rising demand and unmet inflation-driven costs. This represents a significant shortfall—the actual deficit is eight times the budgeted projection—indicating either over-optimistic planning assumptions or weak implementation capability.
findings.matters: Failed delivery of planned savings indicates weak financial management and planning capability; lenders must assess whether management can execute efficiency plans and whether future financial projections are reliable.
findings.figures: £3.133 million (unachieved savings), £8.233 million actual vs £1.000 million budgeted
findings.quote: This is a result of increasing costs to the IJB due to rising demand for services, alongside the non-delivery of approximately £3.133 million of identified savings plans.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Plan for the Year Ending 2025-26 and Update on Recommendations from 2024-25
findings.headline: The IJB faces a £38 million medium-term funding deficit from 2026/27 to 2030/31, with a current-year deficit of £8.233 million requiring partner authority top-ups.
findings.detail: The audit plan identifies financial sustainability as the only significant wider-scope risk. The 2025/26 budget projected a £1 million deficit but actual monitoring shows £8.233 million deficit. The Medium-Term Financial Strategy (2026/27-2030/31) projects a £38 million cumulative funding gap. Partner authorities (Moray Council and NHS Grampian) must provide additional annual contributions for the IJB to break even, and the auditors note that current transformation and savings plans may be insufficient to bridge the identified gap.
findings.matters: The IJB is funded by Moray Council and NHS Grampian, so structural deficits require ongoing partner contributions that squeeze council budgets and threaten financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £8.233 million (2025/26 deficit), £38 million (2026/27-2030/31 funding gap), £1.000 million (budgeted 2025/26 deficit)
findings.quote: The MTFS shows the IJB is facing significant and increasing overspends against future forecast budgets and the funding deficit over the period is projected to be £38 million.

findings.headline: Digital strategy is not yet developed and must align with Transformation Strategy for either to succeed
findings.detail: The auditor notes that work on the Digital Strategy is at an early stage. The council recognises that digital development is extensive and complex (lack of integrated systems, range of IT systems), and that the Digital Strategy must align with the Transformation Strategy. A new strategy is intended to be reported in autumn 2025, but this is not yet in place.
findings.matters: Digital transformation is often a prerequisite for service and cost transformation. If the digital roadmap is not aligned with the savings-delivery roadmap, neither will succeed on time. The absence of a strategy until autumn 2025 means the council is now (August 2025) mid-year with one major pillar undefined.
findings.figures: Digital discovery investment: £0.200m from reserves; new digital strategy to be reported autumn 2025
findings.quote: Work on the Digital Strategy is at an early stage but must align with the Transformation Strategy for both strategies to be successful.

findings.headline: Staffing and capacity constraints are slowing transformation delivery, particularly in a rural council
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that capacity is 'a significant barrier', and the rural nature of Moray 'adds to complexity when recruiting'. The council is using transformation reserve funding to hire specific resource, but there is a risk that 'too much time is being spent on developing plans which is taking away focus from implementation'. A middle management structure review is scheduled for later 2025.
findings.matters: If the council cannot attract and retain the skilled people needed to drive transformation, it will not meet its savings targets. This is a structural constraint specific to rural councils and harder to fix than a generic organisational problem.
findings.figures: Transformation reserve being used to fund specific project resource; rural council; middle management review scheduled H2 2025
findings.quote: To provide the level of transformational change required, the Council need change leaders, service specialists and additional project resource. Capacity is a significant barrier for the Council, and the rural nature of the Council adds to complexity when recruiting.

findings.headline: Transformation Strategy approved only in April 2024 and implementation is still being embedded
findings.detail: The strategy that is meant to close a 10-year £41m gap is very new. The auditor notes work is ongoing to implement and embed it. The previous improvement programme (IMP) was judged by the Controller of Audit to be 'unlikely to deliver the scale of transformation required', and the auditor has identified that pace of change remains a key issue from the March 2024 Best Value Assurance Report.
findings.matters: The council is betting everything on a nascent strategy with a track record of slower change than required. There is material delivery risk and governance risk if phase 3 (not yet defined) does not identify sufficient savings.
findings.figures: Transformation Strategy approved April 2024; Phase 2 ongoing; Phase 3 in development; prior IMP judged 'unlikely to deliver scale of transformation required'
findings.quote: The Transformation Strategy and Corporate Plan were only approved in April 2024 and work is ongoing to implement and embed these strategies.

findings.headline: Council historically over-relied on reserves to balance budgets; this pattern must not resume
findings.detail: For years, Moray covered budget shortfalls by drawing down reserves rather than delivering transformation. 2024/25 saw budgeted use of £10.225m but actual use of only £6.477m, suggesting forecasting difficulty. The auditor explicitly recommends the council must not revert to this approach, but transformation delivery is unproven at the required scale.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know if the council has genuinely shifted to sustainable delivery or simply delayed the inevitable reserve draw-down. The shift away from reserves is recent (2025/26 is the first balanced budget in years) and fragile if savings don't land.
findings.figures: 2024/25: £10.225m budgeted vs £6.477m actual; 2023/24: £15.423m budgeted vs £14.211m actual; Transformation reserve balance: £5.4m
findings.quote: In recent years, the Council have utilised reserves balances to balance the budget. The Council have recognised that this was not a sustainable approach.

findings.headline: Multiple transformation projects are behind schedule, jeopardising delivery of planned savings
findings.detail: In the most recent monitoring report (January 2025), of nine projects in the Transformation Strategy, five were rated amber or red for being behind schedule, and two were not meeting budget expectations. The auditor notes the council needs to regularly review whether timescales remain achievable and the impact delays may have on future savings.
findings.matters: If transformation projects that are meant to deliver £10.9m in savings slip further, the council faces a shortfall with no backup plan. The auditor has already flagged this as requiring urgent review and decision-making.
findings.figures: 5 of 9 projects behind schedule; 2 not meeting budget expectations; 1 not meeting objectives
findings.quote: Several transformation projects are behind schedule and the Council need to review projects regularly to confirm whether timescales remain achievable and the impact this may have on future savings.

findings.headline: Council faces a £41.4 million budget gap over 10 years with only partial savings identified
findings.detail: The council requires £10.905 million in efficiency savings over three years (2025/26–2027/28) to achieve financial balance. Only £7.9m have been identified for 2025/26, and £1m each for 2026/27 and 2027/28, leaving £2m unidentified. Longer-term projections show a mid-range budget gap of £41.365 million to 2034/35, though under pessimistic assumptions this could reach £107.5 million.
findings.matters: A lender assessing Moray's long-term sustainability needs to know whether identified savings will actually deliver, and whether the remaining £2m can realistically be found without reverting to reserve drawdowns that have historically plugged gaps.
findings.figures: £10.905m required 2025/26–2027/28; £7.9m identified for 2025/26; £41.365m budget gap over 10 years (mid-range); £107.5m budget deficit (pessimistic scenario)
findings.quote: efficiency savings totalling £10.9 million are required over the next three years (2025/26 – 2027/28). The Council have approved £7.9 million of savings for 2025/26 and £1.0 million for financial years 2026/27 and 2027/28. The Council aim to identify the remaining savings during 2025.

findings.paper_title: Transformation Strategy Development – Progress to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Across all programmes, the council reports ongoing challenges in securing resources and service capacity.
findings.detail: Section 6.6 states: 'There continue to be challenges in securing resources and service capacity to progress projects.' While allocation of dedicated project resources is showing impact in some areas (smarter working, learning estate), 'Resourcing at Council level is being considered as part of the Phase 2 structural review.' This indicates systemic capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Resource constraints across the transformation programme suggest the council may struggle to deliver planned savings and efficiencies; this affects both financial forecasts and operational delivery capability.
findings.figures: 20 projects in programme; 18 with green aggregated RAG status; resource issues flagged across multiple projects
findings.quote: There continue to be challenges in securing resources and service capacity to progress projects. However, the allocation of project resources to specific projects is showing impact with projects such as smarter working and learning estate showing good progress.

findings.paper_title: Transformation Strategy Development – Progress to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: LED and Solar PV energy projects constrained by spend-to-save principle, limiting upfront investment and design capacity.
findings.detail: Both energy efficiency projects note identical concerns: 'Continues to be concern around future programme which relies on spend to save principles which limits expenditure in advance of approved project.' The LED project specifically notes: 'Design work having to be undertaken at no cost or funded from wider revenue budgets.' Both projects rely on external support for design due to in-house resource reduction.
findings.matters: The council's capital efficiency programmes are being slowed by inability to fund design and development costs upfront; this delays realisable energy savings and increases dependence on external design support.
findings.figures: LED: £218k revenue, £38k savings, target March 2028; Solar PV: £333k revenue, £53k savings, target March 2028; both rely on spend-to-save project approval
findings.quote: Continues to be some concern around future programme which relies on spend to save principles which limits expenditure in advance of approved project. Design work having to be undertaken at no cost or funded from wider revenue budgets.

findings.paper_title: Transformation Strategy Development – Progress to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Just Transition funding outcome still pending; council awaiting ministerial decision with report to Council not until 30 September.
findings.detail: The £3.2m Just Transition project had its bid shortlisted (8 June 2026) and is in due diligence, but final ministerial approval is still pending. The report states: 'Officers awaiting final funding outcome following ministerial consideration. Expected late June/early July.' This 3+ month delay in decision-making creates uncertainty for planning. The project also lists as a risk: 'Risk that funding is not made available in subsequent years to support delivery of projects.'
findings.matters: A significant transformation project remains contingent on external funding not yet confirmed; multi-year funding sustainability is also uncertain.
findings.figures: £3.2m project funding sought; bid submitted 8 May 2026; shortlisted 8 June 2026; decision expected late June/early July but not yet received as of report date
findings.quote: Risk that funding is not made available in subsequent years to support delivery of projects.

findings.paper_title: Transformation Strategy Development – Progress to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Levelling Up Fund programme lost its SRO and Programme Manager; new SRO only in place from 1 June.
findings.detail: The £18.3m Levelling Up 3 project (30% complete) experienced staff turnover at senior level. The report notes: 'Staff resource challenges, previous SRO and Programme Manager have left. New SRO in place from 1 June and acting Programme Manager post to be appointed internally until permanent post recruited (approx. August).' This creates resourcing risk during the delivery phase.
findings.matters: Turnover in programme leadership during delivery phase increases execution risk; the council is also managing concurrent staffing challenges across multiple major programmes.
findings.figures: £18.3m Levelling Up 3 budget; programme 30% complete; includes multiple sites (Gordon Arms, Auction Mart, Sawmill, Central regeneration, South Street)
findings.quote: Staff resource challenges, previous SRO and Programme Manager have left. New SRO in place from 1 June and acting Programme Manager post to be appointed internally until permanent post recruited (approx. August).

findings.paper_title: Transformation Strategy Development – Progress to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Moray Growth Deal programme (£104.4m) faces amber budget and objectives ratings due to flat government funding against inflationary pressures.
findings.detail: The 8-project Growth Deal programme has amber ratings on both budget and objectives. The report directly states: 'With flat Government funding, inflationary pressures could affect the ability of projects to deliver some or all of their outputs.' The council is attempting mitigation through fixed-price agreements and value engineering fallbacks.
findings.matters: A major investment programme on which the council's economic development strategy rests is at risk of scope reduction or delivery shortfalls; lenders need certainty on the ability to deliver intended economic benefits.
findings.figures: £104,416k total funding; 2026/27 grant offer £12.3m (capital) and £749k (revenue); 7 projects in delivery, 1 still to be scoped
findings.quote: With flat Government funding, inflationary pressures could affect the ability of projects to deliver some or all of their outputs.

findings.paper_title: Transformation Strategy Development – Progress to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Depot and Stores Rationalisation project schedule now amber due to resource constraints and expanded scope.
findings.detail: The project was updated from green to amber schedule status. The report states: 'The schedule has been updated to AMBER to reflect increasing delivery pressures and emerging resource constraints.' The scope has expanded to include Archives and Records Storage. This creates pressure on the Full Business Case timeline with 'a risk of delivery slowdown within 6-8 months.'
findings.matters: A major asset rationalisation programme (targeting £3.4m capital savings) now at risk of delay; lenders need assurance that planned capital receipts and revenue savings will materialise on schedule.
findings.figures: £7.5m project cost, £210k revenue saving, £3.4m capital saving, delivery target September 2028
findings.quote: The schedule is now AMBER due to increased demands from expanded scope and existing commitments, creating pressure on the FBC timeline and a risk of delivery slowdown within 6 - 8 months.

findings.headline: IT and cyber security risk remains at very high level (20); potential recovery costs could be substantial and unbudgeted.
findings.detail: The IT risk score is unchanged at 4x5=20 (very high). The register states: 'Intelligence in relation to recent successful cyber-attacks has highlighted that the disruption to the affected organisations can be widespread. It is also likely that significant costs will be incurred during recovery, and that the full restoration of business operations can take months, if not years to complete.' Controls include cyber resilience team and accreditations, but the risk 'cannot be discounted.'
findings.matters: A cyber incident could disable council operations for extended periods and incur substantial unbudgeted recovery costs; this is a tail-risk with potentially significant financial impact beyond normal budgeting assumptions.
findings.figures: IT risk score 4x5=20 (very high); no cost estimates for cyber incident recovery provided
findings.quote: It is also likely that significant costs will be incurred during recovery, and that the full restoration of business operations can take months, if not years to complete.

findings.headline: Moray Integration Joint Board creates unquantified demand-led financial obligation with no clear mitigation.
findings.detail: The register flags 'uncertainties around the council's current and future funding obligations to the Moray Integration Joint Board' as explicitly adding to financial risk. The council notes it is 'working closely with and seeking assurances from the Moray Integration Joint Board to ensure, so far as is practicable, that the financial contribution to be made from Council resources does not exceed budget projections,' but no specific action or resolution is described, and the uncertainty remains acknowledged.
findings.matters: IJB health and social care spending is demand-driven and often grows faster than council budgets; unquantified obligations create unmanaged exposure for a lender assessing the council's financial sustainability.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided; described as adding to financial risk
findings.quote: Uncertainties around the council's current and future funding obligations to the Moray Integration Joint Board add to this risk.

findings.headline: Financial risk reduced to 16 but remains very high; 2026/27 balanced budget masks unresolved medium-term pressure.
findings.detail: The council set a balanced 2026/27 budget through improved Scottish Government settlement, Council Tax rises, and transformation savings. However, the risk score remains at 4x4=16 (very high). The register explicitly states that 'longer-term financial planning projections note that further Council Tax rises and additional savings will be required going forward.' Future pressures include inflation impacts, geopolitical events affecting costs, and 'limitations on availability of capital funding for asset maintenance and renewal.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has identified a path to sustainability beyond the 2026/27 balanced budget or faces a structural deficit requiring either spending cuts or further income rises.
findings.figures: Financial risk score reduced from 5x4=20 to 4x4=16; balanced budget achieved for 2026/27; savings targets identified through 2028/29
findings.quote: Longer-term financial planning projections note that further Council Tax rises and additional savings will be required going forward.

findings.headline: Flow-into care more than doubled in 2025 (31 children) compared to 2024 (14 children), exhausting internal resources.
findings.detail: During 1 April 2024 to 31 October 2025, 45 children were accommodated. In 2024 this was 14 children (13 families); in 2025 this rose to 31 children (27 families including large family groups). The report states 'the flow-into care during the last two financial years has been higher than in preceding years resulting in internal resources being exhausted and severe budgetary pressures.' There is further risk: 'another large family is on the edge of breakdown and other young people could be accommodated by the Children's Hearing system over which we have no control legally.'
findings.matters: Sustained demand increase creates both immediate cost pressure and unpredictable further accommodation needs. The Children's Hearing system can mandate accommodations without council control.
findings.figures: 31 children accommodated in 2025 vs 14 in 2024; 45 children total in 18 months; 41 of 45 affected by 3 or more risk factors
findings.quote: In 2025, 31 children were accommodated representing 27 families, (4 family groups including large family groups). In 2024, 14 children were accommodated which represents 13 families, (1 family group of 3).

findings.headline: Whole Family Wellbeing Fund (£619,000 per annum) has no guarantee beyond financial year 2026/27, risking prevention programs.
findings.detail: The primary funding for early support and prevention services is the WFWF, currently £619,000 per annum for 2025/26 and 2026/27. The report explicitly states: 'the funding is annual and there is no guarantee beyond financial year 2026/27.' The Children and Families Centre hub-and-spoke model, which is intended to reduce future OOA care costs, is dependent on this funding continuing.
findings.matters: Time-limited grant funding creates sustainability risk. If funding ceases, prevention capacity falls and flow-into-care pressures will increase further, driving higher OOA costs.
findings.figures: £619,000 per annum 2025/26 and 2026/27; £277,254 to £315,133 per annum cost of Children and Families Centre hub-and-spoke model
findings.quote: Funding is provided by the WFWF, through the Council's General Revenue Grant, so families receive support at the right time... A significant challenge within the funding requirements is sustainability – the funding is annual and there is no guarantee beyond financial year 2026/27.

findings.headline: At the start of 2024/25, no budget was set for Residential Care and Continuing Care, leaving them as unbudgeted pressures.
findings.detail: When children's services moved to the IJB in 2023/24, the budget structure fragmented into five separate elements. At the start of 2024/25, 'there was no budget provision for Residential Care and Continuing Care but some budget for Disability and Foster Care. Thus, Residential Care and Continuing Care had no budget and became a financial pressure for the partnership.' This reflects systemic budget-setting weakness.
findings.matters: Shows budget planning did not account for all care categories and reflects governance/integration weakness. These unbudgeted categories are now driving overspends.
findings.figures: Residential Care budget: £0; Continuing Care budget: £0 at start of 2024/25
findings.quote: At the start of the financial year there was no budget provision for Residential Care and Continuing Care but some budget for Disability and Foster Care. Thus, Residential Care and Continuing Care had no budget and became a financial pressure for the partnership.

findings.headline: The council warns: 'the financial position going into 2026/27 remains tight. Ongoing action will be needed to bring spending in line with available funding and to maintain financial stability'
findings.detail: In the risk section, the council's own assessment is explicit: repeated budget pressures have not been resolved. The council relied on non-recurring items to balance 2025/26 and will face the same structural gap in 2026/27. The language ('remains tight', 'ongoing action will be needed', 'maintain financial stability') signals the council believes itself to be on a knife-edge and vulnerable to any adverse movement in demand, income, or funding.
findings.matters: This is the finance team's own honest assessment: structural spending pressures are unresolved, reserves are at minimum, and the budget is fragile. For a lender, this is a yellow flag. The council is managing crisis-to-crisis rather than addressing root causes.
findings.figures: Net overspend £230,000; non-recurring items exceed recurring savings by material amount
findings.quote: The outturn position for 2025/26 shows that a number of services are still under financial pressure, particularly from demand-led costs. While these have been managed during the year, this has relied on one-off savings, and other underspends that are not expected to continue. This means there is limited flexibility to deal with unexpected costs or in-year pressures. As a result, the financial position going into 2026/27 remains tight. Ongoing action will be needed to bring spending in line with available funding and to maintain financial stability.

findings.headline: The council's share of Moray Integration Joint Board overspend is £3.38m, with additional £650k staff regrading costs on top, and 'underlying demand pressures remain'
findings.detail: The Moray IJB (health and social care, 30% of total council spend) overspent by £7.2m, with the council's share being £3.38m (47%). The council also incurred £650,000 of additional staff regrading costs outside the IJB provision. The report states: 'While underlying demand pressures remain.' The council budgeted £3.4m just to cover the anticipated IJB overspend, meaning Health & Social Care is now a structural budget hole, not a one-time pressure.
findings.matters: Health and social care spending is growing faster than the council can fund it. The council must now build a £3.4m+ IJB pressure into every forward budget, compressing discretionary spending. This is a demographic time-bomb that lenders must price into refinancing risk.
findings.figures: MIJB overspend £7,196,896; council share £3,382,541 (47%); additional staff regrading costs £650,000; provision budgeted £3,400,000
findings.quote: At Q3 the Moray Integration Joint Board (MIJB) was forecasting an overspend of £8,233,574, with the Council responsible for 47% of this amount, equating to £3,869,780. In recognition of the recurring financial pressures within the MIJB, the Council had included a provision of £3,400,000 within the 2025/26 budget to support its anticipated share of the overspend.

findings.headline: Winter maintenance costs surged to £2.95m (£1.12m overspend) following a severe winter, with no clear plan to handle climate volatility
findings.detail: Roads Management Winter Maintenance overspent by £1,123,000, 'following a particularly severe winter'. This is weather-driven and outside the council's control, yet it shows how vulnerable the tight budget is to external shocks. The council notes operational pressures within Roads and Fleet services remain ongoing. With winter severity unpredictable and reserves at minimum, this kind of pressure will force cuts to other services if repeated.
findings.matters: This is a demand shock the council did not plan for and could not absorb without reserve impact. For a lender, it shows how little room the council has for volatility in costs that are largely outside its control (weather, energy, national pay awards).
findings.figures: Winter Maintenance overspend £1,123,000; total Roads overspend £650,000; Winter Maintenance actual £2,947,000 vs budget £1,824,000
findings.quote: Roads Management reports an overspend of £650,000 at year end. This is primarily driven by Winter Maintenance costs, with an overspend of £1,123,000 following a particularly severe winter, worsening the Q3 position.

findings.headline: Free reserves remain at £6m (the statutory minimum) with no headroom for unforeseen pressures, while earmarked reserves fell by £1.68m
findings.detail: Free general reserves remained flat at £6,000,000, which the council states is 'the minimum level of reserves that can be held... in terms of the Council's financial reserves policy'. Earmarked reserves fell from £29.3m to £27.6m (a £1.68m reduction). The council explicitly warns: 'This means there is limited flexibility to deal with unexpected costs or in-year pressures.' The report notes the council is at the statutory floor and has no buffer.
findings.matters: Operating at minimum free reserves with declining earmarked reserves removes any shock absorber for demand volatility, pay awards, inflation, or interest rate moves. A single bad quarter forces the council back to the lender.
findings.figures: Free reserves £6,000,000 (minimum threshold); earmarked reserves £27,604,000 (down £1,680,000 year-on-year); total reserves £33,604,000 (down from £35,284,000)
findings.quote: The balance on free general reserves (ie excluding DSM and ear-marked reserves) as at 1 April 2025 was £6,000,000. This is the minimum level of reserves that can be held on free general reserves in terms of the Council's financial reserves policy.

findings.headline: Only 75% of approved savings were achieved; £1.41m of planned savings failed and underlying recurring pressures are masked by non-recurring items
findings.detail: The council approved £7.1m of savings for 2025/26. Only £5.36m were achieved (75.5%). £1.41m of savings were assessed as 'unachievable' (red). The report explicitly states: 'While the overall position has improved since Q3, this largely reflects non-recurring variances. The underlying position across many services remains constrained.' Vacancy savings of several hundred thousand pounds across services are identified as 'non-recurring' and 'not expected to continue'. The council relied on one-off items and timing differences to offset structural budget gaps.
findings.matters: Failed savings targets combined with reliance on non-recurring items (vacancy delays, one-off income) means the 2026/27 budget will start with a structural deficit. This is a pattern of fiscal drift: savings don't land, spending pressures accumulate, and reserves become the balancing item.
findings.figures: £7,102,000 approved savings; £5,361,000 achieved; £1,407,000 unachievable (red); £334,000 deferred (amber)
findings.quote: Savings are allocated to service budgets during the year. Where savings are no longer considered achievable, they are either removed (shown as red) or deferred to future years (shown as amber)... Savings achieved total £5,361,000. A further £334,000 has been deferred to future years (amber), while £1,407,000 has been assessed as unachievable (red).

findings.headline: Non-Domestic Rates reliefs overspent by £557,000 and the council identifies this as a recurring structural pressure with no solution
findings.detail: NDR reliefs overspent by £557,000, described as reflecting 'increased demand and changes in relief claims'. The report notes this as a 'key pressure' that remains 'ongoing' and highlights it as one of 'a number of demand-led and operational pressures' that 'remain within service budgets'. The council acknowledges these pressures 'will require ongoing management in 2026/27' but offers no plan to address them.
findings.matters: This is an income-side pressure the council cannot control. NDR relief claims are statutory obligations. A £500k+ recurring pressure that grows year-on-year signals shrinking financial headroom and potential future reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £557,000 overspend on NDR reliefs; identified as recurring
findings.quote: The most significant pressure relates to NDR reliefs, which overspent by £557,000, reflecting increased demand and changes in relief claims.

findings.headline: Out of Area education placements overspent by £1.72m with no clear resolution, representing a major recurring financial risk
findings.detail: Out of Area placements overspent by £1,720,000 in 2025/26. The report identifies this as 'a major financial risk' dependent on existing placements and new demand in 2026/27. Education and Out of Area as a whole overspent by £2,313,000 after reserves transfers. The paper repeatedly flags demand-led education pressures as the single largest recurring problem, yet provides no mitigation strategy beyond monitoring.
findings.matters: An uncontrolled, recurring spend pressure of this scale indicates weak demand management in a major budget area. For a lender assessing refinancing risk, this shows the council cannot control its largest cost drivers.
findings.figures: £1,720,000 overspend on Out of Area placements; £2,313,000 overspend in Education and Out of Area after transfers; identified as 'major financial risk'
findings.quote: The most significant pressure within the service relates to Out of Area placements, which overspent by £1,720,000. This remains a major financial risk, with the recurring element dependent on existing placements and any new demand arising during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Three of seven planned asset management actions from 2024/25 remain incomplete due to conflicting priorities, with completion now deferred to Q3 2027/28
findings.detail: The 2024/25 plan identified seven key tasks. Only four have been completed; three remain in progress. Specifically, the review of Asset Management Plans and related updates has stalled due to conflicting priorities. This work is now bundled into a broader holistic review scheduled for Q3 2027/28.
findings.matters: Slippage on planned asset management actions suggests resource constraints and competing operational pressures, raising questions about the council's capacity to execute planned transformation and efficiency programmes.
findings.figures: 4 of 7 planned actions completed; 3 remain in progress; completion deferred 18+ months
findings.quote: The Corporate Asset Management Plan for 2024/25 included seven key tasks. To date, four have been completed and three are in progress. Conflicting priorities have resulted in little progress by way of reviewing the status.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account viability was reassessed in 2024 following interest rate increases, indicating pressure on the council's self-financing housing programme
findings.detail: The Housing Business Plan was reviewed in 2023, then refreshed in 2024 specifically because of significant interest rate increases. The HRA must continue substantial investment to meet mandatory Scottish Housing Quality Standard and energy efficiency standards while managing higher debt servicing costs.
findings.matters: Rising debt servicing costs are compressing the HRA's financial capacity to fund statutory housing quality and energy efficiency obligations, potentially narrowing flexibility to manage other pressures.
findings.figures: Interest rate increases triggered 2024 HRA reassessment
findings.quote: A review of the Housing Business Plan was carried out in 2023 to assess the capacity of the Housing Revenue Account to deliver the housing service's ongoing investment priorities, and this was refreshed in 2024 following significant increase in interest rates.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure is capped due to affordability constraints, forcing deferral of planned investments including fleet replacement
findings.detail: The council is applying a pro-rata cap on capital spending across all programmes to maintain affordability. As a direct consequence, the Zero Emission Fleet Replacement Strategy approved in April 2024 has been placed on hold. Instead, the council is extending replacement lifespans for light vehicles and prioritising only heavy vehicles and plant replacement. This indicates tightening capital headroom.
findings.matters: Deferred capital investment and extended asset replacement cycles increase operational risk, defer decarbonisation commitments, and may signal narrowing financial flexibility for new borrowing.
findings.figures: Zero Emission Fleet Strategy implementation on hold; light vehicle replacement lives extended
findings.quote: implementation of the strategy is currently on hold due to capital affordability pressures and will be reviewed as part of future fleet and capital planning exercises. The priority is now being given to the replacement of heavy vehicles and plant assets, with replacement lives for light vehicles, including pool cars, being extended in response to current capital funding constraints.

findings.headline: Best Value audit found the corporate asset management plan was out of date and outcomes weren't being reported, flagging governance weakness
findings.detail: The 2025/26 Best Value audit identified that Moray's Corporate Asset Management Plan had not been reviewed since December 2024 and covered only a single year rather than multi-year planning. More significantly, the council had not reported on outcomes achieved from the existing plan. This compliance gap required formal management response and remedial action.
findings.matters: An auditor-identified governance gap in asset management planning raises questions about the council's control framework for managing a significant asset base and planning its financial commitments.
findings.figures: Plan not reviewed since December 2024; covers only 2024/25 instead of multi-year period
findings.quote: The thematic review found that whilst there was good work happening within asset management the CAMP had not been reviewed since December 2024 and is out of date. The current version of the CAMP only covers a single year (2024/25) and does not consider the longer term. Furthermore, the Council had not reported on the outcomes of the existing CAMP and therefore it is unclear what actions have achieved.

findings.headline: Ten-year capital plan shows affordability breach projected for 2031/32, requiring phased spending caps despite current headroom
findings.detail: The 10-year indicative plan shows the affordability indicator (financing costs to net revenue budget) breaching the 10% threshold in 2031/32 at 10.00% in original plan. Spend has been capped in a phased approach to maintain affordability limits. A full review of long-term borrowing affordability is scheduled for Q3 2026/27.
findings.matters: Long-term affordability breach signals borrowing constraints will tighten from 2031/32 onwards, limiting capital capacity and potentially affecting service investment in the medium term
findings.figures: 2025/26 affordability indicator: 7.23% (internal) / 8.97% (external); 2026/27 projected 6.70% (internal) / 8.41% (external); 10-year plan shows 2031/32 at 10.00% (original) / 9.97% (revised)
findings.quote: The 10-year indicative plan for 2026-36 indicated a breach of the affordability indicator in 2031/32. As such, spend was capped in a phased approach to maintain affordability limits.

findings.headline: Moray Growth Deal programme underspent by £5,434,000 due to tender delays and funding partner engagement challenges
findings.detail: Underspend driven by delays in tender process for Elgin Town Hall, pausing of Grant Lodge to enable focus on external fundraising, and delays in planning process for South Street and Dallas Dhu housing projects. The council has revised the spend profile following recently approved change management plans.
findings.matters: Growth Deal is time-limited partnership funding; persistent slippage risks clawback or loss of match funding, and signals challenges in delivering regeneration partnerships
findings.figures: £5,434,000 underspend (£5,421,000 spent of £10,855,000 budget = 50% delivery); revised 2026/27 spend down £1,494,000 but Scottish Government releasing additional £3,539,000
findings.quote: The Cultural Quarter was underspent due to delays in the tender process for Elgin Town Hall and the pausing of Grant Lodge to enable the team to focus on external fundraising.

findings.headline: Learning Estate programme experiencing major project reprofiling with Cullen Primary, Alves Primary and Elgin High School all delayed or scope-reduced
findings.detail: The £5,041,000 Learning Estate underspend reflects multiple delays: Cullen Primary School upgrade reprofiled to 2026/27, Alves Primary being retendered to secure best value, Mortlach Primary starting late, and Elgin High School capacity extension reduced from new build to repurposing existing space. The council notes this reflects a rolling ten-year programme but the scale of movement suggests planning challenges.
findings.matters: School capacity extensions are forward-planning investments; delays and scope reductions may indicate insufficient pupil place provision or rising costs constraining plans
findings.figures: £5,041,000 underspend on Learning Estate (£9,610,000 spent of £14,651,000 budget = 66% delivery)
findings.quote: This was mainly due to the Cullen Primary School upgrade being reprofiled into 2026/27, the Alves Primary fabric upgrade being retendered to secure best value and maximise market interest, the late start to Mortlach Primary refurbishment, and the Elgin High School capacity extension being reduced from a new build extension to the repurposing of existing space.

findings.headline: Housing delivery partner withdrew from South Street project, requiring appointment of replacement delivery partner
findings.detail: The South Street project, which is fully LUF-funded, had to be paused when the original housing delivery partner withdrew. A new delivery partner has now been appointed and the project has resumed. This demonstrates vulnerability to third-party withdrawal.
findings.matters: Third-party partner withdrawal is a material delivery risk, particularly for complex multi-partner schemes; it reveals exposure to private sector confidence and willingness to deliver
findings.figures: South Street is fully Levelling Up Fund-funded; specific budget impact not separately quantified but included in £2,639,000 LUF underspend
findings.quote: South Street, which is fully LUF-funded, has resumed following the appointment of a new delivery partner after the original housing partner withdrew.

findings.headline: Multiple Levelling Up Fund projects cancelled or significantly delayed due to value for money concerns, design constraints and stakeholder objections
findings.detail: Railway Bridge and Moss Street Active Travel projects are no longer progressing due to poor value for money and stakeholder objections. Cooper Park was delayed by affordability concerns but has since improved. Gordon Arms Hotel asset transfer delayed by legal issues. South Street resuming after original housing partner withdrew.
findings.matters: LUF grants are time-limited; cancelled projects mean funding may be returned or reallocated, and withdrawal of third-party partners demonstrates execution risk on multi-partner schemes
findings.figures: £2,639,000 underspend on Levelling Up Fund (£2,478,000 spent of £5,117,000 budget = 43% delivery)
findings.quote: Projects at Railway Bridge and Moss Street Active Travel are no longer progressing due to poor value for money, design constraints, and stakeholder objections.

findings.headline: Project teams are small with minimal resilience; staffing vacancies and departures directly impact delivery pace
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies staffing capacity as a critical slippage driver. Industrial Units work was delayed by staffing vacancies; team departures cause momentum loss; limited supporting service capacity creates bottlenecks. The council faces challenges in recruiting and retaining staff for these specialist roles.
findings.matters: Persistent understaffing in capital delivery limits the council's ability to execute its capital programme, creating ongoing risk of further slippage and cost escalation
findings.figures: Specific examples: £90,000 underspend on Industrial Units due to vacancies; various projects delayed by key staff departures
findings.quote: Project teams are often small with limited resources. In instances where a key member of the team leaves there is a notable impact on the pace of delivery, with momentum often lost.

findings.headline: Capital delivery is 65% against plan, with £45,128,000 of approved expenditure carried forward to future years
findings.detail: The council spent £32,596,000 against an amended 2025/26 capital plan of £50,564,000. This represents significant slippage across multiple programmes including £5,041,000 (Learning Estate), £5,434,000 (Moray Growth Deal) and £2,639,000 (Levelling Up Fund). The council is operating on a three-year rolling plan but projects are still being managed with single-year mentality.
findings.matters: Persistent underspend raises questions about delivery capability, creates inflationary pressure on deferred projects, and delays public benefit realisation
findings.figures: £32,596,000 spent of £50,564,000 budget (65% delivery); £45,128,000 carry forward; £18,247,000 carry forward to 2026/27
findings.quote: Capital spends to the year end 31 March 2026 were £32,596,000 against the amended Capital Plan of £50,564,000, representing a delivery of 65%.

findings.headline: Garmouth Viaduct span removal costs now exceed original £500,000 estimate and will require formal tendering
findings.detail: The Spey Viaduct partially collapsed in December 2025. After Stage One of the removal contract, actual costs are now higher than the £500,000 estimate. The works will require formal tender as costs exceed the Small Works Framework limit. A report to council will request additional funds; timing depends on delivery schedule.
findings.matters: This is emergency infrastructure repair that must proceed regardless of cost, creating an unbudgeted liability and signalling cost estimation risks on complex projects
findings.figures: Originally estimated £500,000; actual costs now exceed this; £538,000 allocated from 2026/27 general capital grant but additional funds will be required
findings.quote: Stage One, including the method statement, programme and cost estimate have been completed, and the costs are more than the original estimate of £500,000.

findings.paper_title: Moray Integration Joint Board Draft Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Integration of Children's, Families and Justice services incomplete; target August 2026
findings.detail: The register identifies that complete integration of delegated Children's, Families and Justice services is not yet finished. An organisational review is underway. Until complete, there is acknowledged governance exposure across these services.
findings.matters: Incomplete governance integration of delegated statutory services is a control weakness; the services remain at risk of operating outside the IJAB's framework until integration is complete.
findings.figures: Target completion: August 2026
findings.quote: Complete integration of Children's, Families and Justice. Organisational Review and Change process underway.

findings.paper_title: Moray Integration Joint Board Draft Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Workforce strategy and plan not yet delivered; refresh timescale unconfirmed
findings.detail: The risk register identifies that the workforce plan requires review and update but notes 'awaiting SG' (Scottish Government guidance) with target date marked TBC (to be confirmed). The workforce risk is rated Medium but the lack of an agreed delivery plan for what is acknowledged as a critical capacity issue creates uncertainty.
findings.matters: Unresolved workforce capacity directly affects service delivery resilience and cost pressures; unconfirmed timescales for a strategic plan suggest either delay or that the scope is being re-scoped.
findings.figures: Risk 3 (Workforce) rated Medium; refresh timeline TBC
findings.quote: Review and update of the Workforce Plan – awaiting SG TBC TBC

findings.paper_title: Moray Integration Joint Board Draft Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: 2024/25 Internal Audit opinion downgraded to 'Limited Assurance' with delays in audit recommendations
findings.detail: The Internal Audit Annual Report (June 2025) concluded 'Limited Assurance' rather than adequate assurance. Weaknesses were noted in contract management, digital tracking arrangements, and delays in implementing audit recommendations. This represents the control environment assessment.
findings.matters: Limited audit assurance is a red flag for governance and control weaknesses; delayed implementation of audit fixes prolongs exposure to known risks and suggests control execution problems.
findings.figures: 2024/25 audit opinion: Limited Assurance (reported June 2025)
findings.quote: the 2024/25 Internal Audit opinion of 'limited assurance' with delays in recommendations and weaknesses noted in contract management, digital and tracking arrangements

findings.paper_title: Moray Integration Joint Board Draft Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Very High financial risk with savings plan slippage across 2025/26
findings.detail: The financial risk is rated Very High (unchanged from January 2026), driven by in-year pressures and savings not landing as planned. The register explicitly flags that a savings programme slippage was presented to the board in January 2026. Demand growth is outpacing available funding, particularly in high-cost care packages and children's services.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a local authority can execute its financial plans; acknowledged slippage in a recovery plan signals execution risk and potential future deficits.
findings.figures: Very High rating (untreated 5×5=25, current 3×5=15); risk unchanged from January 2026
findings.quote: in year pressures, savings slippage and recurrent cost growth outpacing available funding, including high-cost care packages and demand growth in adults and children's services. Slippage in savings programme for 2025/26 presented to MIJB January 2026.

findings.headline: Planning income running £182,000 behind budget (18.2% shortfall) in Q1 due to lower application volumes
findings.detail: Planning fee income is underperforming by £182,000 in the first quarter due to lower planning application volumes. This is treated as a controllable income pressure rather than a timing issue.
findings.matters: Income shortfalls from discretionary activities signal softer demand in the local economy and reduced development activity, which also affects other council income streams and may persist if economic conditions weaken further.
findings.figures: £182,000 shortfall on planning income at Q1
findings.quote: The Service is reporting an overspend of £187,000 at Q1, mainly due to Planning income being £182,000 below budget to date as a result of lower planning application fee income.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves drawn down by £3.3m in Q1 to fund approved commitments and transformation activities
findings.detail: In the first quarter alone, £3,268,000 was released from earmarked reserves, including £1,079,000 from Transformation Reserve and £982,000 from other earmarked reserves. This is a significant draw on reserves in just three months.
findings.matters: Heavy Q1 reserve releases to fund ongoing activities suggest the budget is not self-sustaining and the council is relying on reserve drawdown to balance spending. If this run-rate continues, reserves could be significantly depleted within 12-18 months.
findings.figures: £3,268,000 released in Q1; £1,079,000 from Transformation Reserve; £982,000 from other earmarked reserves; total reserves at 30 June down from £27,603,000 to £24,335,000
findings.quote: During Q1, £3,268,000 was released from reserves, including £1,079,000 from the Transformation Reserve, £982,000 from other earmarked reserves, £751,000 of Pupil Equity Funding and £155,000 of DSM balances.

findings.headline: General reserve held at absolute minimum required level of £6.0m with no buffer for unexpected pressures
findings.detail: The council's general reserve stands at £6,000,000 as at 30 June 2026, which is identified as the minimum level required under the Financial Reserves Policy. This provides no cushion for unexpected pressures and limits financial flexibility.
findings.matters: A general reserve at absolute minimum means the council has no buffer for any unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls, and any further financial deterioration would require emergency action or deficit funding.
findings.figures: £6,000,000 general reserve (minimum required level); £18,335,000 earmarked reserves
findings.quote: As at 1 April 2026, the balance on the General Reserve was £6,000,000 which is the minimum level required under the Council's Financial Reserves Policy approved by Council on 25 September 2024

findings.headline: Savings programme is only 25.6% delivered at Q1 with four savings totalling £168,000 assessed as unachievable
findings.detail: Of £4,446,000 in approved savings, only £1,141,000 have been posted or are expected to be achieved by Q1. Four savings totalling £168,000 are assessed as red and not expected to be achievable because budget reductions have already been applied. Additional savings remain amber (dependent on later implementation or profiling).
findings.matters: A savings programme that is running at less than 26% delivery at the quarter-end point, with identified red-rated items, indicates a significant risk that the full-year £4.4m savings target will not be met, creating a material budget gap.
findings.figures: £1,141,000 delivered against £4,603,000 total approved savings (24.8%); £168,000 in red-rated savings; £4,446,000 original approved savings
findings.quote: As at 30 June 2026, savings totalling £1,141,000 have been processed or are expected to be achieved during 2026/27. Four savings totalling £168,000 are currently assessed as red and are not expected to be achievable as the equivalent budget reductions have already been applied within service budgets.

findings.headline: Health and Social Care MIJB overspend of £1.7m is part of a continuing trend from prior year
findings.detail: The Moray Integration Joint Board position shows a £1,707,000 overspend at Q1. The overall MIJB position before additional funding was £1,973,000 overspent. The paper explicitly states this reflects ongoing cost pressures and continues the trend reported in the previous year's budget monitoring reports.
findings.matters: A continuing overspend trend in integrated health and social care, year-on-year, indicates structural cost pressures that are not being managed down and raises questions about financial sustainability of this major cost area.
findings.figures: £1,707,000 Q1 overspend; £1,973,000 overall MIJB overspend before additional £9m funding from partners
findings.quote: This reflects ongoing cost pressures within services delivered on behalf of the Moray Integration Joint Board and continues the trend reported in the previous year's budget monitoring reports.

findings.headline: Out of Area Placements overspent by £743,000 due to increased demand for young people requiring placements
findings.detail: Education's Out of Area Placements are running £743,000 over budget in Q1 alone, driven by an increase in the number of young people requiring such placements. The paper identifies this as a significant recurring pressure that continued from the previous year.
findings.matters: Growing demand for specialist education placements is a pressure the council cannot easily control or reduce, and if sustained across 12 months could create a material budget overspend with no clear mitigation strategy outlined.
findings.figures: £743,000 overspend within the £522,000 total Education variance, representing an increase in placements required
findings.quote: The main pressure relates to Out of Area Placements, which are overspent by £743,000 to date due to an increase in the number of young people requiring placements. This remains a significant recurring budget pressure.

findings.headline: Q1 overspend of £2.3m (3.2%) driven by ongoing Health and Social Care and education placement pressures
findings.detail: The council is overspent by £2,299,000 against budget to date, with the largest pressures in Health and Social Care delivered through the Moray Integration Joint Board (£1,707,000) and Education Out of Area Placements (£522,000). The paper notes these are recurring pressures consistent with those identified at budget setting.
findings.matters: An overspend this early in the year indicates structural cost pressures rather than timing issues, and the reliance on central provisions to absorb them suggests the council may face a significant full-year outturn problem.
findings.figures: £2,299,000 overspend (3.2%), Health and Social Care MIJB £1,707,000, Out of Area Placements £522,000, actual spend £74,059,000 against budget of £71,760,000
findings.quote: Itemised spend to 30 June 2026 was £74,059,000 against budget to date of £71,760,000 resulting in an overspend to date of £2,299,000. Material variances relate to Health and Social Care services delivered on behalf of the Moray Integration Joint Board (£1,707,000 overspend) and the Council's share of Ous of Area Placements within Education budgets (£522,000 overspend).

findings.headline: The 2026-27 budget is already unbalanced and depends on unproven mitigating actions
findings.detail: The paper states the 2026-27 budget was 'presented as a balanced budget position, through the use of partner contributions, and a challenging savings plan'. However, the recurring overspend of £6.2m discovered at year-end is £1.8m worse than the budget assumed. The Senior Management Team have 'put in place mitigating actions' but these are not detailed and the paper warns 'There is a big risk for 2026/27 onwards to achieve a financial balance.'
findings.matters: A new year budget that was sold as balanced but which inherits an undisclosed additional £1.8m structural cost is credibility damage. If mitigations fail, the board will deficit-spend.
findings.figures: Recurring overspend discovered £1,832,873 worse than budgeted; earmarked reserves only £3,010,434
findings.quote: The out turn has a £2,096,308 non-recurring underspend in staffing, however, due to ongoing challenges with recruitment means that although classed as non-recurring there is still an element of this underspend that will be achieved in 2026/27. There is a big risk for 2026/27 onwards to achieve a financial balance.

findings.headline: Mental Health service has unresolved consultant recruitment issues and is using out-of-area placements as stopgap
findings.detail: Mental Health overspent by £654k, with £302k spent on agency locums for consultants and £195k on purchase of care, including out-of-area packages. The paper notes 'lack of resource locally especially around autism and neurodiversity' and states 'Work is currently ongoing reviewing out of area packages to repatriate them to Moray', implying current provision is suboptimal and costly.
findings.matters: Inability to recruit permanent mental health consultants creates both cost pressure (locums) and access/quality risk. Out-of-area placements signal service failure.
findings.figures: Mental Health overspend £654,343; agency locums £302,457; purchase of care including out-of-area £195,385
findings.quote: This budget is currently under pressure due to the recruitment issue for consultants and an increase in demand for services, including out of area packages as there is a lack of resource locally especially around autism and neurodiversity.

findings.headline: Children's services overspent £0.8m, driven by rising residential and external fostering placement costs
findings.detail: The Children, Families & Justice budget overspent by £793,663 due to residential care placements (£418k), external fostering (£496k), and out-of-area residential (£297k). The board notes the market is under scrutiny for excessive profiteering and that 'availability of the correct care provision is a national challenge'. A long-term strategy to reduce flow into care has been approved but is not yet delivering savings.
findings.matters: Children's placement costs are driven by statutory duty and growing family breakdown. If the board cannot control these costs or has no capacity to prevent children entering care, deficits will persist.
findings.figures: Children overspend £793,663; residential continuing care £418,127; external fostering £495,610; out of area residential £297,272
findings.quote: The costs of care have been rising significantly, availability of the correct care provision is a national challenge, and the market is under scrutiny with consultation for possible legislation on excessive profiteering.

findings.headline: Agency and locum staffing costs are preventing achievement of vacancy-based savings targets
findings.detail: The board set a vacancy target saving of £1.135m but achieved only £0.762m due to agency staff and interim positions required to maintain service. Community nursing regraded staff (band 6 to band 7) and recruited to long-vacant posts using bank staff, then could not achieve expected savings. Mental Health spent £302k on agency locums due to consultant recruitment difficulties.
findings.matters: If the board cannot fill permanent posts affordably, it is trapped paying higher agency rates. This is a cost-control risk and suggests workforce planning or capability issues.
findings.figures: Vacancy target saving plan £1,135,000; achieved £762,000; Mental Health agency locums £302,457; Community Nursing regrading from band 6 to band 7
findings.quote: Use of bank staff /locum to provide required cover for vacancies/sickness and from the historic incremental drift and efficiency targets imposed. Overspends can be due to the use of bank staff /locum to provide required cover for vacancies/sickness

findings.headline: Permanent and nursing care demand is rising faster than budget, with 9% growth in nursing placements
findings.detail: The board noted that permanent care resident numbers rose from 533 to 555 (4.13%), but nursing placements increased from 396 to 432 (9.1%), a shift toward higher-cost care. The Older People budget overspent by £1.9m driven by home care and nursing placement cost growth. The paper flags this as an ongoing trend in Scottish IJBs.
findings.matters: Demographic-driven demand for high-cost care is structural and recurs every year. If the board cannot manage this within budget, it faces escalating deficits unless services are rationed or costs controlled.
findings.figures: Permanent care residents increased 533 to 555 (4.13%); nursing placements increased 396 to 432 (9.1%); Older People budget overspend £1,933,488
findings.quote: For permanent care, there was an overall increase in resident numbers from 533 to 555 (4.13%) Within this there has been a reduction in residential placements and an increase in nursing placements 396 to 432 (9.1%)

findings.headline: Savings plan delivered only 57% of target, with £4m of planned reductions unachieved
findings.detail: The board planned £9.5m of savings for 2025-26. Actual delivery was £5.4m including reductions in overspends. Multiple projects marked as 'Red' risk (unlikely to succeed) include internal care reviews, care home redesigns, and digital efficiencies. The paper acknowledges that £3m of planned savings were carried forward to 2026-27.
findings.matters: If the board cannot execute a planned savings programme, it signals weak delivery capability and a worsening deficit for 2026-27 when those unachieved savings were already needed.
findings.figures: Full year savings plan £9.5m (later £9,469,000); achieved £5.4m (£4,343,000 savings plus £1,031,000 overspend reduction); £3m carried forward to 2026-27
findings.quote: Estimated savings delivered to date total £5.4m against planned full year savings of £9.5m, with £3m being carried forward into 2026/27

findings.headline: A structural overspend of £6.2m will carry into 2026-27 with no general reserves to absorb it
findings.detail: The core services overspent by £5.4m in 2025-26, but the paper reclassified variances and found an underlying recurring overspend of £6.2m — £1.8m worse than budgeted for 2026-27. The board has no usable general reserve; only £3m in earmarked reserves remain. The paper warns this additional cost cannot be met from reserves.
findings.matters: A council unable to fund recurring cost pressures from reserves faces forced cuts to services or may need external support, both signals of financial distress.
findings.figures: Recurring overspend £6,226,395; total reserves £3,010,434 (all earmarked, no general reserve); 2026-27 budgeted recurring overspend was £4,393,522 but actual is £6,226,395
findings.quote: This additional cost cannot be met from reserves going into 2026/27. There are earmarked reserves of £3,010,434 and no general reserve. With no general reserves the additional cost and any emerging budget pressure will have to be funded from additional savings or from recommissioning other activities.

findings.headline: No earmarked reserves are budgeted to be drawn despite five years of consecutive deficits
findings.detail: Table 5 shows 'Use of earmarked reserves - - - - -' (dashes) across all forecast years, indicating zero reserves deployment. This signals either no accessible reserves or a decision to preserve them; neither option supports deficit closure.
findings.matters: Reserves are the normal buffer for temporary deficits; their non-use suggests either they are depleted or the authority is rationing them for crisis use, indicating financial fragility.
findings.figures: Table 5: 'Use of earmarked reserves - - - - -' (all years)
findings.quote: Use of ear marked reserves - - - - -

findings.headline: Demographic shift to an ageing population with declining child population will drive service demand growth the framework cannot fund
findings.detail: Moray's population is forecast to decline 0–15 by 13% but grow pension-age population by 15% over 2026–2036. The framework budgets £1m–£1m demographic pressure annually but Table 3 shows total pressures of £15–22m; demand growth is not funded.
findings.matters: Foreseeable demographic pressure is not funded; the authority will face political and legal pressure to maintain services for elderly population while budgets are frozen.
findings.figures: Children population projected to fall 13%; pension-age population to grow 15% by 2036
findings.quote: Demographic pressure – pressure continues on this budget for the foreseeable future, due to increases in complexity and demand.

findings.headline: High-cost individual packages in Learning Disability, Children and Mental Health are expected to rise but are budget-fixed after 2026/27
findings.detail: The framework budgets £1.86m for 2026/27 high-cost packages but caps growth at £1.5m annually thereafter, despite acknowledging 'significant packages expected'. This suggests the budget assumes cost containment rather than demographic or need-driven growth.
findings.matters: If complex cases continue to emerge beyond the £1.5m assumption, this becomes a pressure point that forces cuts to lower-cost services or increases the deficit.
findings.figures: High-cost packages: £1,860k (2026/27), then £1,500k annually 2027/28–2030/31
findings.quote: High Cost Individuals – there are significant packages expected in 2026/27 for Learning Disability, Children and Young People and Mental Health service, but beyond then we will need to consider different care models

findings.headline: Funding is committed only on a one-year basis, preventing medium-term planning certainty
findings.detail: Scottish Government and partner council/health board funding are confirmed only one year at a time. This prevents multi-year planning and creates risk that funding could be cut or changed mid-framework, forcing emergency rebalancing.
findings.matters: One-year funding commitments mean the £240m budget is not guaranteed; a policy shift could leave the authority unable to meet statutory obligations.
findings.figures: Framework covers 5 years but funding commitment is annual
findings.quote: Scottish Government funding settlements to our funding partners, Moray Council and NHS Grampian are currently on a one year only basis, this has a direct impact on the funding to the MIJB.

findings.headline: Audit Scotland has flagged integration authorities across Scotland as facing a critical financial position
findings.detail: The document cites Audit Scotland's February 2026 bulletin, which states that 'IJBs across Scotland are facing a critical financial position, with costs and demand rising faster than available resources'. This is independent external audit confirmation of sector distress.
findings.matters: External auditor assessment of sector-wide critical position indicates this is not a local planning issue but a systemic problem with no obvious policy fix in sight.
findings.figures: Scottish Government resource fiscal gap forecast to widen from £963m (2026/27) to £2.6bn (2029/30)
findings.quote: These updates also align with the national picture set out in Audit Scotland's February 2026 bulletin, which highlights that IJBs across Scotland are facing a critical financial position, with costs and demand rising faster than available resources

findings.headline: Unmet care needs now and pandemic health debt will create demand surge risk
findings.detail: The document states the authority is 'acutely aware' of 'unmet need in both assessment and delivery of care'. Combined with acknowledged pandemic health debt from services not fully resumed, this signals suppressed demand that could emerge and worsen deficits.
findings.matters: Latent demand from unmet need and service backlog could materialize mid-forecast, forcing emergency cuts or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: No quantification of unmet need or health debt provided
findings.quote: We are acutely aware of the current impact on the citizens of Moray in respect of the level of unmet need we are experiencing in both assessment and delivery of care.

findings.headline: Prescribing budget is volatile and represents 13% of core spend with no control mechanism identified
findings.detail: The risk section explicitly flags GP prescribing as 'extremely volatile in nature' and capable of 'substantial adverse variances'. At 13% of budget, a 5% variance would add £1.5m to the deficit. No mitigation is detailed.
findings.matters: An uncontrollable volatility representing one-eighth of budget threatens the entire deficit-reduction plan if volumes or prices move.
findings.figures: Prescribing budget pressure 2026/27: £1,708k; ongoing annual pressure £1,000k
findings.quote: GP Prescribing – represents around 13% of the MIJB core budget. It is well documented that the Prescribing budget can be extremely volatile in nature with volume and price increases potentially leading to substantial adverse variances.

findings.headline: Cost pressures of £38m over 5 years with no contingency if transformation targets are missed
findings.detail: The framework explicitly states the predicted cost rise requires 'significant transformation to achieve financial balance', but offers no specifics on what transformation or contingency if it fails. Pay, prescribing volatility, and complex care packages drive £19–22m of annual pressure.
findings.matters: A finance plan that depends on undefined transformation without fallback plans indicates high execution risk; if transformation stalls, the deficit widens immediately.
findings.figures: Total budget pressures 2026/27: £19,054k; pay inflation 3% Council/2% NHS; prescribing 13% of core budget
findings.quote: The predicted rise in costs over the term of this framework is £38.017 million, which will require significant transformation to achieve financial balance.

findings.headline: Structural annual deficits of £9.3m–£9.9m across the forecast period with no reserves solution planned
